tasks.short: Show a customer how to use a home espresso machine or grinder sold in the shop.

steps.what: Customer asks about an espresso machine or grinder on sale
Barista asks how the customer drinks coffee and picks a machine to show
Barista checks the model's manual or spec sheet for settings and features
Barista demonstrates grinding, dosing, tamping, extraction and milk steaming on the espresso machine
Customer tries a shot under the barista's guidance
Barista explains cleaning and descaling of the machine to the customer
Barista prepares a brew and care guide for the model: photocopies manual pages today; after the change the one-page guide is generated from the model record
Barista checks the guide before handing it over: the customer's machine and grinder model and, for e-mail, the address the customer gives
Barista hands the printed guide over or e-mails it to the customer

tasks.design: Keep one record per machine and grinder model in the {DOCS} store (key settings, starting recipe, cleaning schedule, manufacturer video link) and show it on the counter tablet. A small generator turns the record into a one-page brew and care guide with a QR code to the videos; the barista checks it is for the customer's model and hands it over or sends it by {EMAIL} to the address the customer gives.
tasks.previous_blocker: Manuals were long and differed per model; staff relied on memory and photocopies.
tasks.enabler_now: A simple record per model and a document template are quick to build and keep.
tasks.still_hard: The hands-on demonstration and tasting is the point and cannot be shortened.
tasks.human_edge: Reading the customer's skill, letting them taste the difference and building confidence at the machine.

ambition.what: A free 20-minute dial-in session two weeks after purchase, booked from the e-mailed guide.

tasks.altitude: Nothing changes in decision rights; the barista spends less time looking up settings and writing tips.

reach.task: Show customers how to use rented equipment
reach.learn: Whether a per-model record and one-page guide work for rental items.

evidence.claim: A document template can generate a one-page guide from a structured record per product model.
Sending the guide by e-mail needs the customer's address for that purpose only; marketing needs separate consent under GDPR.

assumptions: Boundary: from the customer's question to the guide handed over; the sale itself is outside.
Input contract: per model the key settings, starting recipe, cleaning schedule and video link, produced by the head barista from manufacturer material; fallback is the paper manual.
Customer time is outside the barista's savings.

The demonstration, explaining care, checking and handing over the guide keep their full time. s3 keeps 50 because one record replaces paging through the manual. s6g keeps 30 for printing and a glance at the generated guide.
unknowns: How many machines the shop sells per month.
Whether manufacturers allow linking their videos.
research_questions: Do buyers who get a written guide come back with fewer questions?

incremental.description: Barista updates a model record when settings or recipes change.
Head barista adds records for new models.

approvals.approved_version: The brew and care guide for the named machine and grinder model exactly as checked by the barista in s6c, handed over or e-mailed once to the address the customer gave for it; any change needs a new check.

time_saved_range_pct.basis: Low: staff know the few models well and seldom open the record, so s3 keeps 80 (3.7); high: the record replaces the manual for every demonstration (7.5).

tasks.savings_basis: 100 focal-role baseline hours; external labour excluded; incremental focal work deducted once; provisional

tasks.short: Check coffee, milk and retail stock, order from roaster and dairy, receive deliveries and stock shelves.

steps.what: Barista counts beans, milk, cups and retail coffee bags at closing
Barista works out quantities and writes the order list in the shared notebook
Barista checks the final roaster order: beans and retail bags, quantities and the roaster
Barista e-mails or messages the order to the roaster today; after the change the workflow sends the checked roaster lines
Barista checks the final dairy order: milk types, quantities and delivery day
Barista messages the order to the dairy today; after the change the workflow sends the checked dairy lines
Supplier delivers the order with a delivery note
Barista receives the delivery, checking dates and milk temperature
Barista checks quantities against the order
Barista stocks milk, beans and retail products, oldest first, pricing retail bags

tasks.design: A tablet stock form, set up in the till's stock module ({OTHER}) or the {OPS_SYSTEM}, estimates bean and milk use from drinks sold and recipe grams, so the barista counts only key lines; the system drafts the order from par levels. The barista adjusts the draft and checks each supplier's lines, and a workflow sends each checked order to its supplier by {EMAIL} or {PARTNER_PORTAL}, and the delivery check ticks off the same order lines.
tasks.previous_blocker: Usage was never linked to sales, so every line was counted and every order worked out by hand.
tasks.enabler_now: Tills record each drink sold, recipe tools hold grams per drink, and par-level ordering is a standard stock feature.
tasks.still_hard: Waste, spills and events break the usage estimate; deliveries, cold chain checks and shelving stay physical.
tasks.human_edge: Knowing a busy weekend or a market day is coming and spotting a milk delivery that is too warm.

ambition.what: Milk ordered daily against sales so less milk is thrown away.

tasks.altitude: The barista confirms a drafted order instead of building it; the store manager sets par levels and the budget.

reach.task: Check stock and list shortages for the manager
reach.learn: Whether the same sales-based draft works for food items.

evidence.claim: A recipe tool stores the ingredients of each recipe and costs them from ingredient prices.
Stock modules can draft orders from par levels, counts and sales-based usage.
Chilled dairy must be received and kept cold under food hygiene rules; details follow national rules.

assumptions: Boundary: from the closing count to stock on the shelves; supplier invoices are outside.
Input contract: item list with par level, supplier and order unit, produced by the store manager; recipe grams per drink from the recipe record; fallback is the paper order list.
The barista orders within a weekly budget set by the store manager; orders above it are blocked and go to the manager outside this flow.
Supplier time is outside the barista's savings.

Receiving and checking dates and temperature (s5) and both order checks keep their full time. s6 keeps 80 because only finding the paper order drops; noting each difference is still the barista's own record. s1 keeps 80 because beans and milk are estimated from sales and the barista counts the other lines.
unknowns: Whether suppliers take orders by portal or only by e-mail or phone.
Whether drink recipes are recorded in grams.
research_questions: How far does sales-based milk use drift from counted use in a week?

already_counted.description: Barista reviews and adjusts the drafted order.

incremental.description: Barista corrects usage drift with a full count once a week.
Store manager keeps par levels and supplier details current.

approvals.approved_version: The roaster order with items and quantities exactly as checked by the barista in s3c, sent once by {EMAIL} or {PARTNER_PORTAL} to the roaster; any change needs a new check.
The dairy order with items, quantities and delivery day exactly as checked by the barista in s3e, sent once by {EMAIL} or {PARTNER_PORTAL} to the dairy; any change needs a new check.

time_saved_range_pct.basis: Low: usage estimates drift, so the barista keeps counting every line and adjusts many drafted quantities, s1 keeps 100 and s2 keeps 60 (16.0); high: estimates hold and the draft is used (23.0).

tasks.savings_basis: 100 focal-role baseline hours; external labour excluded; incremental focal work deducted once; provisional

tasks.short: Tell customers about coffee blends, origins, roasts and how drinks are prepared.

steps.what: Customer asks about a blend, its origin or how a drink is made
Barista describes the coffee blend, origin, roast and taste notes from memory
Barista reads the roaster's bag label or info sheet when unsure
Barista checks the allergen folder for plant milks and syrups
Barista suggests a brew method, grind and ratio for home use
Barista offers a small taste of the filter or espresso

tasks.design: One record per blend and drink in the recipe system ({OTHER}) holds origin, process, roast, taste notes, brew recipe and allergens; the counter tablet and a QR code on the shelf and menu show it. A template prints a small brew card per blend for customers buying beans.
tasks.previous_blocker: Blend details sat on roaster sheets and in staff memory; allergen folders were separate from the drink list.
tasks.enabler_now: Recipe tools hold allergen data per recipe, and QR menus show item descriptions and allergens to guests.
tasks.still_hard: Describing taste is personal and changes per batch; the record must follow the roaster's new lots.
tasks.human_edge: Matching a coffee to the customer's taste and making the conversation enjoyable.

ambition.what: Customers who read the origin and brew card by QR while waiting, in their own language.

tasks.altitude: Nothing changes in decision rights; fewer trips to labels and folders.

reach.task: Explain how dishes are prepared and which allergens they hold
reach.learn: Whether the same allergen lookup serves café and restaurant staff.

evidence.claim: A QR menu linked to the till shows item descriptions and allergen information to guests.
A recipe tool stores allergen and dietary data per recipe.
Guests must be informed about 14 allergens in unpacked food; spoken information is allowed with a notice.

assumptions: Boundary: from the customer's question to the answer, advice or tasting; the sale is outside.

Input contract: per blend the origin, process, roast date range, taste notes and brew recipe from the roaster's info sheet; per drink the allergens, produced by the head barista; fallback is the bag label and folder.
No model writes answers; the tablet shows the record.
Customer time is outside the barista's savings.

Describing, advising and tasting are conversation and keep their time; s5 keeps 90 because the printed brew card replaces writing the recipe down for the customer. s3 and s4 keep 50 because one record on the tablet replaces the bag label and the separate allergen folder.
unknowns: How often blends and lots change.
Whether the roaster supplies info sheets in a reusable form.
research_questions: Which questions do customers ask most that a card could answer?

incremental.description: Barista updates blend records when a new lot arrives.
Head barista keeps drink allergen data current.

time_saved_range_pct.basis: Low: few blends and staff know them, so the record halves fewer lookups (s3 and s4 keep 75) and no brew cards are used (5.0); high: the record and cards are used as designed (12.8).

tasks.savings_basis: 100 focal-role baseline hours; external labour excluded; incremental focal work deducted once; provisional

tasks.short: Make chalkboards, posters and table cards that advertise products, offers or events in the shop.

steps.what: Store manager decides the product, offer or event to advertise
Barista gathers product name, price, dates and event times
Barista writes and draws the chalkboard or lays out a printed sign
Store manager checks the final sign: product, price, dates and wording against the promotion record, and where it goes
Barista puts the sign up in the window, at the counter or on tables
Barista takes down or changes signs when the offer or event ends

tasks.design: A sign generator in the {DOCS} store with house-style templates (poster, table card, chalkboard text, social post) fills product, price and dates from the till's promotion record ({OTHER}). The manager approves the final print file on a phone, and a calendar reminder on the end date tells the barista to take the sign down; chalkboards stay hand-drawn from the generated text.
tasks.previous_blocker: Each sign was made by hand, and promotion details lived in chat messages, not a record.
tasks.enabler_now: Template tools fill fixed fields and export print and social formats in minutes.
tasks.still_hard: Hand-drawn chalkboards are part of a coffee shop's look and stay manual; a template only helps printed signs.
tasks.human_edge: Drawing a board that makes people stop, and choosing words that fit the shop.

ambition.what: A sign and social post for every new single-origin or small event on the day it starts.

tasks.altitude: The barista spends less time on layout and more on the hand-drawn boards that matter; the manager approves from a phone.

reach.learn: Whether the same template and approval serve restaurant specials.

evidence.claim: Template tools can fill product, price and date fields and export print and social formats.
Prices shown on signs must be the full selling price including VAT under EU price indication rules.

assumptions: Boundary: from the promotion brief to the sign taken down; deciding promotions is outside.
Input contract: promotion record with product, price, start and end date, produced by the store manager in the till; fallback is the chat message.
Scenario: about half of signs are printed and half are hand-drawn chalkboards.
Store manager time is outside the barista's savings.

Putting signs up keeps its full time. s3 keeps 60: half of signs are printed and lose most of their layout work, the hand-drawn half keeps its time. s6 keeps 85 because the end-date reminder replaces walking round to find expired signs; taking them down stays.
unknowns: How many signs the shop makes per month and how many are hand-drawn.
research_questions: Do printed signs or hand-drawn boards sell more of a promoted product?

incremental.description: Barista fixes template layouts that break with long names.
Store manager keeps promotion records and templates current.

approvals.approved_version: The final print file or chalkboard text with product, price and dates exactly as checked by the store manager in s4, put up once at the named spot in the shop; any change needs a new check.

time_saved_range_pct.basis: Low: most signs stay hand-drawn chalkboards and promotion records are often incomplete, so s3 keeps 80 and s2 keeps 70 (16.0); high: half of signs printed from complete records (31.3).

tasks.savings_basis: 100 focal-role baseline hours; external labour excluded; incremental focal work deducted once; provisional

role.altitude: The barista keeps making drinks, demonstrating and talking coffee; order lists, label lookups and sign layout shrink.
reach: Counter workers' stock checks and orders
Waiters' allergen answers from the same record
skills_to_grow: Keeping product and blend records accurate
Confirming drafted orders with judgement on events and weather
Using sign templates without losing the shop's character
role.ambitious_version: A barista who runs ordering from a drafted list, keeps the shop's coffee knowledge in one record, and offers buyers a follow-up brewing session.
